subject: Confirming TTFT targets and SSE chunk cadence for Acme POC
messages:
From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa@redwood.com>
To: Marta Ruiz <marta.ruiz@acme-retail.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 6 Nov 2025 15:04:00 -0800
Subject: Re: POC kickoff — performance notes and next steps

Hi Marta — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and the concrete next steps we agreed so everyone is aligned before the POC starts: 

Summary of performance targets discussed
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): target median <= 300 ms for short prompts (<= 80 tokens), p95 <= 500 ms.
- Streaming behavior: SSE preferred, client expects initial token within TTFT window above and then regular chunks during generation.
- Chunk cadence: target ~50–120 ms between server-sent chunks for an average token rate; acceptable upper bound 250 ms for slower segments.
- Concurrency and throughput: initial load is 50 concurrent active streams (sessions) with peak throughput ~120 req/s; long term target 250 concurrent sessions.
- Model/response size assumption: average responses ~120 tokens, occasional up to 1,000 tokens for long-form.

Action items we committed to
1) Redwood will run a short synthetic test that measures socket connect + first byte latency and chunk cadence using SSE (we'll share the harness).
2) Acme will provide a short set of representative prompts (3–5) covering short/medium/long responses — thanks for attaching acme_perf_requirements.pdf.
3) Technical workshop: 30m deep-dive to validate metrics and discuss fallback behavior (SSE -> WebSocket or poll) on Friday, 11/14.
4) We'll produce a proposed canary configuration (batching, concurrency limits, quantization profile) and a draft SOW for legal.

Notes/clarifications
- For clarity, our first-token strategy attempts to stream the first decoded token as soon as it is available (we don't wait to finish full-chunk assembly). That is how we meet TTFT in streaming scenarios; we will include a breakdown (scheduling, model decoding, network) in the test report.
- Cost impact: enabling aggressive low-latency settings (smaller micro-batches, lower packing) can increase GPU token cost; we'll include estimated delta in the canary proposal.

Attachments: acme_perf_requirements.pdf (you sent), redwood_test_plan_template.pdf (attached for test harness).

If that all looks right, I'll schedule the workshop and kick off the synthetic test tomorrow.

Best,

Thanks Vanessa — this is very helpful. A couple quick clarifying questions before the workshop: 

1) SSE vs WebSocket: our client infra preferably uses SSE due to simpler reconnection semantics. If we see sporadic dropped chunks, do you have an out-of-the-box fallback to WebSocket or is that something we'd need to build?

2) Chunk cadence tolerance: you said 50–120 ms is the target. Is the 250 ms acceptable upper bound per-chunk guaranteed under your Dedicated offering, or just a soft expectation for Hosted during high-load? We need to include a p99 SLA tolerance in our internal write-up.

3) For the first token: can you confirm that the first byte will be sent before tokenization/processing on the client (i.e., you stream decoded tokens, not pre-buffered text)? Will there be a protocol-level header indicating chunk boundaries?

4) Cost: happy for you to include an estimated delta. Also, can you confirm if the test harness can run from our AWS region (us-east-1) to give realistic RTT numbers?

I'll get the representative prompts over by EOD and review the SOW draft.

Best,
Marta Ruiz

Hi Marta — quick technical responses inline: 

1) SSE vs WebSocket
- Redwood supports both SSE and WebSocket on Hosted and Dedicated. SSE is our recommended default for simple client stacks; it carries lower operational overhead.
- Fallback: we don't currently auto-fallback from SSE -> WebSocket in the client SDK. For the POC we can provide a small client wrapper (example in the test harness) that attempts SSE and retries with WebSocket on repeated failures.

2) Chunk cadence SLA expectation
- For Dedicated (reserved capacity) we can commit to a p95 chunk cadence of <= 250 ms under the agreed concurrency profile; p99 guarantees require contractual SLA language and explicit capacity reservation — we will call that out in the SOW.
- For Hosted, cadence is workload-dependent; during noisy multitenant periods we recommend Dedicated for tight chunk cadence SLAs.

3) First-token behavior and protocol
- We stream decoded tokens as soon as the model decoder emits them; clients receive the first chunk (often 1–3 tokens) as soon as it's available — this is how TTFT is measured.
- Chunk boundaries: SSE events deliver JSON payloads with a sequence id and partial text; the SDK will surface a streaming iterator so you don't need to parse boundaries yourself. We'll include the protocol example in the tech workshop.

4) Test harness and region
- We can run the harness from an EC2 instance in us-east-1 to mirror your environment. We'll include RTT and cold start variation tests.

Proposed quick canary config (for POC):
- Model: open-llama-70B-quant (approx) — example only, will confirm exact family.
- Batching: micro-batches sized to prioritize latency (no packing above 2 requests per micro-batch).
- Concurrency cap for initial run: 50 streams, ramp to 120 req/s sustained.
- Telemetry: per-request TTFT, chunk timestamps, queue delay, GPU decode time.

I'll prepare the harness repo and a test run plan this week and share links.

-Karthik
Staff SRE/SE, Redwood Inference
